clue.text: Unaware of such a blissful state, they say

definitions.text: of such a blissful state, they say

explanation.walkthrough: The second half leans on the saying 'ignorance is bliss': 'they say' points to the proverb, not to a homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking knowledge is the plain sense; the proverb says ignorance is bliss, so someone in that blissful state is uninformed.

clue.text: RA paints unusually one-sided

indicators.note: arranged unusually, so the letters of these two words are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A Royal Academician produces pictures with an odd bias.
explanation.walkthrough: RA (Royal Academician) is fodder here, not an abbreviation to expand: its two letters join PAINTS before 'unusually' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan view favours one faction, so it is biased.

clue.text: Find jumpers with naughty child what a pity

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous youngster
alas is an exclamation of regret

explanation.surface: Someone looking for sweaters alongside a badly behaved youngster sighs in regret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpers' looks like sweaters, a British word for knitwear, but it means leaping animals; 'Find' and 'with' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: These African antelopes are famous for their huge leaps.

clue.text: Growing slender like head of Kipling's Co.?

explanation.definitionFit: Long and thin like a plant stem; also the nickname of the ringleader in Kipling's school stories, the trio of 'Stalky & Co.'

clue.text: Crush the spirit

explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour is to stamp it out; whisky from Scotland is the drink called by the same name.

clue.text: Like what this clue is, needing to hopefully be solved?

definitions.text: Like what this clue is, needing to hopefully be solved?

parts.words: Like what this clue is, needing to hopefully be solved?
parts.note: the clue splits an infinitive with 'to hopefully be', a construction purists condemn as bad grammar

explanation.definitionFit: A sentence that breaks the rules of syntax is faulty in its grammar, as the split infinitive here is said to be.

clue.text: Student of Urdu wandering in tea-garden

indicators.note: the letters wander from their places, so the two words are mixed together

explanation.surface: Someone studying the Urdu language strolls about a garden where tea is served.
explanation.definitionFit: A university student who has not yet taken a first degree.

clue.text: Jeevish. peevish sort in distinctive dress?

parts.note: livery, like liverish, means irritable or bad-tempered
like Jeeves, P. G. Wodehouse's valet, so a manservant

explanation.surface: An irritable butler in the mould of Jeeves wears a striking outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Livery is also the uniform of a household's staff, so the definition reads both ways; the full stop after 'Jeevish' is a printing mark, not part of the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A footman or similar domestic wore the household's own uniform colours.

clue.text: Showing address, road repair takes it

indicators.note: takes means the rearranged letters are followed by the next word, which they pick up
a road under repair is broken up and remade, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The roadworks show a fine address, and the crew mend it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Address' here means dexterity or skill, not a place to send post.
explanation.definitionFit: Being deft and skilful, which is an old sense of the noun address.

clue.text: This school case is for removal

explanation.definitionFit: A Latin grammatical case learnt at school; also an adjective for wearing material away, as with a heat shield.

clue.text: Not well placed among mill workers

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of the words that follow, so they are found within them

explanation.surface: A worker in a textile factory is unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Sick or poorly.

clue.text: Pops round railway terminals and finds tree-nymphs

indicators.note: round means the fathers go around the next letters

parts.note: pop is a familiar word for a father

indicators.note: the terminals of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Fathers walk round the station and spot woodland spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits of Greek myth who live in trees.

clue.text: Start hiking in new year perhaps-destination unimportant

indicators.note: in puts the single letter inside the rearranged letters
perhaps means the letters of the phrase are only one possible order, so they are rearranged
the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A walker sets off at New Year without caring where the trail leads.
explanation.definitionFit: When the destination does not matter, you may go to any place at all.

clue.text: Locks up to deceive, like a common judge

definitions.text: Locks up to deceive, like a common judge

parts.words: Locks up to deceive, like a common judge
parts.note: false locks worn on top of the head, as every British court judge customarily wears

explanation.definitionFit: A hairpiece is false hair, and British judges traditionally wear one in court.

clue.text: People of peculiar orbits around noon

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters surround the single letter
peculiar means strange, so the letters are set out oddly

explanation.surface: Inhabitants of odd planetary paths circle at midday.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Great Britain, a national people.

clue.text: Being at fault, dismissed

explanation.definitionFit: A calculation that is off is in error; in cricket a batsman who is dismissed leaves the field.

clue.text: Could the gardener train it not to ramble?

definitions.text: Could the gardener train it not to ramble?

parts.words: Could the gardener train it not to ramble?
parts.note: a wild hedgerow flower whose name suggests a pet that might be trained not to wander

explanation.definitionFit: A wild climbing briar of hedgerows; ramblers are climbing roses and dogs are trained not to roam.

clue.text: So to get up and manage, one looks into labyrinth

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the words are read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Someone rises and copes, then explores a maze.
explanation.walkthrough: The labyrinth is the inner ear, not a maze.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical instrument for examining the ear canal; the labyrinth is the inner ear.

clue.text: Strike-breaker's queue untidy at the head

parts.note: a rat is a worker who breaks a strike
a queue is a plait of hair hanging down behind, a pigtail

explanation.surface: A scab joins a line of people, looking scruffy up top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queue' looks like a line of people but is the old word for a pigtail.
explanation.definitionFit: Straggly, lank locks of hair are described with this phrase.

clue.text: As in Leo, perhaps, from the deep?

definitions.text: As in Leo, perhaps, from the deep?

indicators.note: perhaps means the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Leo the star sign might be imagined as a big cat risen from the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Leo is a lion; one from the sea is the marine mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: A large eared seal of the ocean, named after the big cat.

clue.text: Caring for issue of others?

parts.note: issue means offspring, so this is caring for children born to other parents

explanation.definitionFit: Describes parents who raise children taken in from elsewhere.

clue.text: He might feign ignorance of Post Office's total

parts.note: PO is short for Post Office, with the possessive S

explanation.surface: A clerk pretends not to know what the counter's takings come to.
explanation.walkthrough: To play this animal is to pretend to be dead or unaware.
explanation.definitionFit: The American marsupial feigns death when threatened.

clue.text: Finest sort of haunt

indicators.note: sort means put in order, so the word's letters are reorganised

explanation.surface: The best kind of place someone frequents.
explanation.definitionFit: Pests or spirits that haunt a place overrun it.

clue.text: Roy, TUC sort, in widespread protest

indicators.note: sort means arrange, so the letters of the two words are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written: TUC is Britain's Trades Union Congress

explanation.surface: A trade unionist called Roy joins a mass demonstration.
explanation.walkthrough: The TUC is the Trades Union Congress, the British federation of unions.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud public clamour of objection.

clue.text: A kicking set of rules, according to Mr Bumble

definitions.text: set of rules, according to Mr Bumble

explanation.definitionFit: The donkey is a kicking beast; Mr Bumble in Dickens's Oliver Twist declares 'the law is a ass'.

clue.text: For Wagnerian hero, standard fails unexpectedly

parts.note: par is the normal or standard level

indicators.note: unexpectedly means the letters turn up in a surprising order

explanation.surface: A Wagner production falls short of normal standards.
explanation.definitionFit: The title knight of Wagner's last opera, who finds the Grail.

clue.text: Forty winks for Tom?

parts.note: Tom is a male cat, so a short doze taken by one

explanation.definitionFit: A brief daytime doze, named as if taken by a cat.

clue.text: Oil put in means trouble using this pigment

indicators.note: troubling something stirs it up, so these letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A painter warns that adding oil spells difficulty with this colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: A water-based wall paint with pigment suspended in it.
